deep.reconstruction:
This page has no computations. It is a programmatic prose draft. It closely matches, often verbatim, the concluding section of Riemann's Göttingen Inaugural-Dissertation, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse' (1851). The verso carries Göttingen magnetometer notes dated May 1850, which fits a 1850–51 date.

Content in modern terms:

(1) Restricting the class of functions. Earlier sections of the dissertation, via the Dirichlet-principle argument, show that a function can be fixed by arbitrary boundary or line conditions. For applications, Riemann now singles out functions that depend on only finitely many parameters. These are functions not subjected to arbitrary conditions prescribed pointwise along lines.

(2) When this happens: his example. Let the domain of z be a surface T spread over the whole infinite plane, once or several times. This is a branched covering of the Riemann sphere, so a compact Riemann surface. On it the function w is allowed only isolated singularities, and these are poles of finite order. That is, w is a meromorphic function on a compact Riemann surface.

The deleted parenthesis states the compactification explicitly: the domain of 1/z should extend from all sides up to the value 1/z = 0. In modern terms, the point at infinity is adjoined, with local coordinate t = 1/z.

(3) Normalising pole order. At infinity, z itself counts as infinitely large of first order. At a finite point z', the reference function is 1/(z - z').

[My gloss:] This means the local uniformizer is 1/z at infinity and z - z' at z'. A function has a pole of order n at z' if it grows like (z - z')^(-n), and at infinity if it grows like z^n. (At branch points one would use a fractional power of z - z'; that refinement is not on this page.)

(4) The claim. The principles developed so far allow such a function to be fully determined independently of any analytic expression for it. From this general basis one can then 'descend' to its various explicit representations.

(5) Programmatic conclusion. The theory of these 'simplest dependence laws between two quantities' is the starting point and the most important part of the theory of complex quantities. Applying them in this generality reveals a harmony and regularity that would otherwise stay hidden. This has proved its worth step by step for algebraic functions, circular (trigonometric) functions, and elliptic and Abelian functions. It widens insight into the laws of analysis and command of its tools.

Underlying idea [my gloss]: a meromorphic function on a compact Riemann surface is determined, up to finitely many constants, by its poles and principal parts. This is the qualitative content later made precise by the Riemann–Roch theorem (Riemann 1857, Roch 1865).
errors: No mathematical errors on the page.

The finite-parameter claim relies implicitly on the Dirichlet principle as used in the preceding sections. Weierstrass later criticised that principle; Hilbert repaired it around 1900. The step is therefore not rigorous by modern standards.

Pole order is normalised only via z and 1/(z - z'). Branch points of a multi-sheeted surface need a fractional local parameter. That is not addressed here, though the dissertation handles it elsewhere.

results.what: Functions defined on a surface spread over the whole (compactified) plane with only finite-order poles depend on finitely many parameters and are determined independently of any analytic expression
results.modern_name: Meromorphic functions on a compact Riemann surface; finite-dimensionality of L(D) (qualitative precursor of Riemann–Roch)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (Dissertation 1851; Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen 1857); Roch 1865 for the full theorem

results.what: Adjoining the point at infinity using the local variable 1/z; order of pole at infinity measured against z, at a finite point against 1/(z - z')
results.modern_name: Riemann sphere / one-point compactification with local uniformizer t = 1/z; order of a pole
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1851); the sphere model is often linked to Neumann (1865)

results.what: Programme: define functions by their singularities and the surface, then descend to explicit expressions (algebraic, circular, elliptic, Abelian functions)
results.modern_name: Riemann's geometric/existence-theoretic approach to function theory

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the published closing section of Riemann's 1851 dissertation, with near-identical wording. The only extras are the deleted parenthesis making the compactification at 1/z = 0 explicit and minor stylistic variants. That is of mild philological interest only.

checkable.asserts: In the local coordinate w = 1/z at infinity, z = 1/w has a pole of exact order 1 (first-order infinity).
1/(z - z') has a simple pole at the finite point z'.
1/(z - z') stays finite (indeed tends to 0) at infinity, so its only pole is at z'.

On the sphere, a function whose only pole is at infinity, of order n, is a polynomial of degree n. It depends on n+1 parameters (here n = 3, with 3 free lower coefficients after fixing the leading one), illustrating the finite-parameter claim.

transcription_corrections: 'eine ohnedies[?] verborgen[?] bleibende Harmonie' should read 'eine ohnedies [corrected from ohnedem] versteckt bleibende Harmonie'. The line break falls inside 'ver-|steckt'.
'und zwar {+nur+} einem Unendlichwerden': the word 'nur' is an interlinear insertion above 'einem'. The reading is correct.
'wobei für ein unendliches z': 'unendliches' appears to replace an earlier word (it looks underlined or overwritten). The reading 'unendliches' is plausible.
Marginal folio number '87' (pencil) at the right edge is not transcribed.
